title: English Confession: receive and rest in Christ — assurance of grace is not faith’s essence
source_text: LIV. Nec alia quoque potuit esse mens eorum qui Confessionem Anglicanam conscripserunt Anno 1647. Etenim praecipuos fidei salutaris actus dicunt esse acceptare & recipere Christum, & in eo solo acquiescere, sive illi soli inniti, ad justificationem, sanctificationem, & vitam aeternam, cap. 14. num. 2. Et praeterea distinguunt fidem salutarem a certitudine quod aliquis sit in Dei gratia, de qua separatim agunt cap. 18. Ubi ut supra notavimus, dicunt illam certitudinem non ita esse de fidei essentia, quin vere fidelis possit ea diu carere. Unde manifestum est, secundum eorum doctrinam, fiduciam illam sensus, quae est haec ipsa certitudo, non esse formalem & proprium actum qui essentiam fidei constituit, quandoquidem fides sine illo, saltem ad tempus subsistere potest: sed fiduciam aliam per quam Christo innitimur, & in eo acquiescimus, ut misericordiam a Deo consequamur.
pass_a_gloss: Nor could the mind of those who wrote the English Confession in the year 1647 have been otherwise. For they say the chief acts of saving faith are to accept and receive Christ, and to rest in Him alone, or to lean on Him alone, unto justification, sanctification, and eternal life, chapter 14, number 2. And besides they distinguish saving faith from the certainty that someone is in God's grace, of which they treat separately in chapter 18. Where as we noted above, they say that that certainty is not so of the essence of faith that a truly faithful person cannot long lack it. Whence it is manifest, according to their doctrine, that that trust of sense, which is this very certainty, is not the formal and proper act which constitutes the essence of faith, seeing that faith can subsist without it at least for a time: but another trust by which we lean on Christ and rest in Him, that we may obtain mercy from God.
pass_b_english: English Confession 1647: chief acts = accept/receive Christ; rest/lean on Him alone for justification, sanctification, life (14.2).
Separates saving faith from certainty of being in grace (ch. 18).
True believers may long lack that certainty — so sense-fiducia is not faith’s formal essence.
